author: blu
body: A reservation that would cross the page WRITES to it rather than raising anything of its own. That is deliberate: the fault handler already routes a guard-page hit to `__out_of_memory`, which reloads RSP before printing and so survives a trampled stack, and reusing it means an overrun reports identically whether it arrived in one jump or a million small ones. A second, differently worded failure path for the same condition is a second thing to keep true.

author: blu
body: The base is READ from the cell the boot code publishes (`guard-page-base-addr`, `Emit/X86_64Boot.codex`) rather than recomputed from the reserve constant, because two derivations of the same geometry drift and the direction this one would drift is permissive. A cell that reads back implausibly is treated as absent: the check is skipped rather than guessed at, so a stale address or an unpublished cell makes this inert instead of tripping on healthy compiles.

author: blu
body: A phase carries the name it is known by. Without it the metrics list is positional, and a reader has to map DECK-4 onto a phase by counting `phase-start` calls in `opening.codex` -- which is how one entry came to hold two ratios that disagreed by a factor of four with nobody able to settle which phase either described. A measurement that needs a decoder ring is a measurement that will be misquoted.

author: blu
body: The write-path bound every guarded phase shares. A phase that reserves a deck passes its ceiling down to whichever loop writes that deck in bulk, and the loop asks this before each item: is there still a guard band's worth of room? A ceiling of zero means unbounded, which is what a caller with no reservation of its own passes.

author: blu
body: This is a WRITE-path check on purpose. check-deck-overflow runs after the phase, which is after a deck that grew into the bivy has already been read back -- so it reports damage rather than preventing it, and it cannot even do that reliably, because phase-measure's own record is allocated on the deck that overflowed.

author: blu
body: A phase whose deck writes go through MANY SMALL deck-record extents is the other case: each extent's exit returns the counter to zero and writes R10 back, so the cell tracks the frontier and deck-short-of is live. SCOPE is that shape (resolve-expr wraps per-pattern-variable results), which is why its guard works.

author: blu
body: Use deck-bound-short-of from inside a phase-wide extent and deck-short-of from outside one. Getting this backwards is silent in both directions: deck-short-of inside an extent never fires, and deck-bound-short-of outside one reads the bivy pointer, which is above every deck ceiling, and fires on the first item.

author: blu
body: Which one a loop is in is a fact about the CODE and not about the phase. RESOLVE, LIFT, LOWER and the PARSE-KEEP copy are all inside theirs and all read R10. CHECK is not, and nothing about CHECK's shape says so: check-chapter issues a bare __deck-exit immediately before check-all-defs and a __deck-enter after it, three lines apart, so the walk between them is bivy-bound and reads the cell. Look for that pair before choosing a predicate; assuming from the phase's name gets it wrong for exactly one phase, and wrong there is a compiler that type-checks one definition and emits nothing.
